title: what your prayer is actually saying
hookLine: seven verses said in every prayer, many times a day, and what they actually say
carry: a conversation, answered line by line

cards: It's said in every unit of every prayer: seventeen times on an ordinary day. Many Muslims learned it by heart as children and could say it half asleep. Ask what it means, line by line, and a lot of people go quiet.
There's a question people really ask: what's the point of praying in Arabic if I don't understand it? Today, the whole thing, in plain English.

teach.b: It's called al-Fatiha, the opening: the first surah of the Qur'an, from a root meaning to open. A key, in Arabic, is a miftah.
Seven short verses. Here they are, in plain words. In the name of God, the Beneficent, the Merciful.
Praise be to God, Lord of the Worlds. The Beneficent, the Merciful. Owner of the Day of Judgment.
You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help. Show us the straight path: the path of those You have favored, not of those who earn anger, nor of those who go astray. That's all of it.
Notice the shape. It opens in yesterday's name.
Then praise, and mercy said twice. Then it turns from talking about God to talking to God: You. And when it finally asks for something, it asks for one thing.
A saying the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ reported from God describes it as a conversation. When someone praying says, praise be to God, Lord of the Worlds, God answers: My servant has praised Me.
Line after line, an answer comes back. So here's the answer to the Arabic question. The words don't change.
Knowing them changes how you say them. Even one line, known while you say it, gives a wandering mind somewhere to stand.

how: Muslims recite al-Fatiha in Arabic in every unit of every prayer, and at many other moments: over the sick, at a wedding, for someone who has died. Many learn it as children, before any other surah.

games.q: what's inside the opening — tap the pairs.
p: God's answer, in a saying of the Prophet ﷺ

s: al-Fatiha is mostly a list of requests
it's mostly praise. it asks for one thing: show us the straight path.
al-Fatiha is said in every unit of every prayer
a saying of the Prophet ﷺ says there is no prayer without it.
the root of fatiha also gives the Arabic word for a key
f-t-h, to open: a key is a miftah.

games.q: someone new to the prayer knows very little Arabic yet. which part does a saying of the Prophet ﷺ say no prayer can be without?
games.why: there is no prayer without al-Fatiha. that's why it's usually among the first things a learner memorizes.

games.q: put the prayer's shape in order.

practice: One breath with the bell. Breathe in. On the way out, say the one request, in Arabic or in English: ihdina s-sirat al-mustaqim.
Show us the straight path. It's the line the whole prayer leans toward.

wordCard.voice: Al-Fatiha. The opening: seven verses, praise first, then one request. Second word on your strand.

orig.note: Arabic: "the opening." from f-t-h, to open, the same root as miftah, a key.

carryVoice: Your line: a conversation, answered line by line. Next time you hear it, you'll know what's being said. Day two, done.
